title: The Crash Impact Database — Overview: when things hit things
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Every crash is a conversation between momentum and structure. A moving object carries momentum — mass times velocity — and when it meets another moving object or a static one, that momentum is redistributed in milliseconds. Some energy becomes motion of the wreckage, some becomes heat and sound, and the rest is absorbed by crushing structure. Engineers study crashes two ways: by crashing real things into real barriers and measuring the violence, and by simulating the impact in software before any metal is bent. This database holds both: test data and the physics that explains it.
capabilities: Momentum and energy: what is conserved and what is lost
Moving vs moving and moving vs static collision families
Physical crash testing and computer simulation side by side
Why milliseconds matter: crash pulse and deceleration

title: The Crash Impact Database — Momentum and energy in collisions
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. In any collision the total momentum is conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only redistributed. Kinetic energy is not conserved: in a perfectly elastic collision it survives, in a perfectly plastic one the objects stick together and the maximum energy is lost to deformation. A 1500 kg car at 15 m/s carries about 169 kilojoules; stopping it in 0.5 meters of crush means an average force near 340 kilonewtons. The crash pulse — deceleration plotted against time — is the signature engineers tune: a long soft pulse saves occupants, a short hard spike injures them.
capabilities: Momentum conservation in every collision

title: The Crash Impact Database — Coefficient of restitution
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. The coefficient of restitution, e, measures bounciness: the ratio of relative speed after impact to relative speed before, from 0 (dead stop, objects stick) to 1 (perfect bounce). It is measured with drop tests — drop a ball from height h, measure the bounce height, and e is the square root of the height ratio. A steel ball on a steel plate scores near 0.9; a lump of clay scores near 0. Real crash structures are designed for low restitution: the energy must die in the metal, not return as rebound. Restitution data is catalogued by material pair, temperature, and impact speed.
capabilities: Restitution from 0 (dead) to 1 (perfect bounce)
Drop-test measurement: bounce height ratios
Material-pair restitution data with conditions

title: The Crash Impact Database — Crash test programs
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Crash test programs crash cars the same way every time so results can be compared. The IIHS runs moderate-overlap and small-overlap frontal tests, side impacts, and roof-strength tests; Euro NCAP scores adult, child, pedestrian, and safety-assist protection out of stars; NHTSA runs full-frontal barrier and side pole tests for its star ratings. Instrumented dummies — Hybrid III and THOR families — record head, neck, chest, and leg loads in every run, and high-speed cameras watch the structure fold at a thousand frames per second. Ratings turn physics into buying decisions.
capabilities: IIHS overlap, side, and roof-strength tests
Euro NCAP star scoring across four protection areas
NHTSA frontal barrier and side pole tests
Instrumented dummies and high-speed camera records

title: The Crash Impact Database — Crumple zones and energy absorption
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. A crumple zone is a structure designed to fail gracefully: longitudinal rails fold in programmed buckles, the engine bay sacrifices itself, and the passenger cell stays rigid. Engineers tune the force-crush curve so the average force stays high enough to stop the car in the available distance but the peak never spikes into injury territory. Load paths carry forces around the cabin — through sills, pillars, and the roof — like a cage. Energy-absorbing foams and honeycomb blocks fill bumpers and door beams, crushing at near-constant force to soak up the last kilojoules.
capabilities: Programmed buckling in longitudinal rails
Force-crush curves: high average, capped peaks
Load paths that route force around the cabin
Foams and honeycombs for constant-force absorption

title: The Crash Impact Database — Impact versus barriers: moving into static
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. The purest crash test is a moving object into a static one. Rigid concrete barriers test the vehicle alone — the wall does not give, so every joule must die in the car. Deformable barriers with aluminum honeycomb faces simulate being hit by another car, sharing the crush between the two. Pole tests drive the car sideways into a rigid pole at 29 km/h to punish weak side structure. Guardrail and bollard tests protect what is behind the barrier rather than what hits it. Each barrier is a different question, and the database records the question with the answer.
capabilities: Rigid barriers: the wall gives nothing
Deformable barriers: simulating the other car
Side pole tests at 29 km/h
Guardrails and bollards: protecting what is behind

title: The Crash Impact Database — Material impact tests: drop and pendulum
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Before whole vehicles are crashed, materials are tested small. Drop towers raise a weight and release it onto a specimen, measuring force against time as the material dents, cracks, or shatters. Charpy and Izod pendulum tests swing a hammer into a notched bar and read the absorbed energy from how high the hammer rises after — the classic measure of toughness versus temperature, revealing the ductile-to-brittle transition in steels. Packaging drop standards (ISTA, ASTM) drop boxed products from specified heights onto specified faces, because the real world drops things too.
capabilities: Drop towers: force-time histories of small specimens
Charpy and Izod pendulum toughness tests
Ductile-to-brittle transition in steels
Packaging drop standards: ISTA and ASTM

title: The Crash Impact Database — Computer crash simulation
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Explicit finite-element codes like LS-DYNA simulate crashes by slicing the vehicle into hundreds of thousands of elements and stepping time forward in microseconds — small enough that a stress wave cannot cross one element per step. Material models encode how steel hardens as it strains and how aluminum tears; contact algorithms stop parts passing through each other. A full-vehicle crash model runs for hours on clusters, and the golden rule is validation: the simulation must reproduce a real crash test's pulse, intrusion, and dummy loads before it is trusted to predict a new design.
capabilities: Explicit finite elements: microsecond time steps
Material models: hardening, tearing, failure
Contact algorithms that keep parts solid
Validation: matching real test pulses before trusting predictions
